newsitem.title: TANZANIA: Tanzanians brace for fuel tax rises.
newsitem.headline: Tanzanians brace for fuel tax rises.

text.p: Tanzanians braced for a rise in fuel prices on Sunday after Finance Minister Daniel Yona announced tax increases in the 1997/98 budget.
Oil industry executives have already held urgent meetings with the government on the implications of the rises, Roger Ivens, head of BP (Tanzania) told Reuters.

In Thursday's budget Yona announced he would reduce the sales tax on premium and regular grade petrol from 30 to 25 percent, but excise duty for premium grade petrol would go up to Tshs 15.85 ($0.025) a litre from Tshs 9.8391.
The basket of taxes on fuel products should contribute an extra Tshs 13.4 billion in government revenue, Yona said.

University academics warned in the independent Guardian newspaper that fuel prices would go up because of the higher taxes and said any increase in duties on industrial diesel fuel would be passed on to the ailing manufacturing sector.
Premium grade petrol currently retails in the Tanzanian capital for about Tshs 420 per litre and Tshs 328 per litre for diesel oil, though fuel prices are higher in rural areas.
Excise duty on JET A1 aviation fuel would increase from Tshs 10.65 to Tshs 15.78 per litre and industrial diesel oil from Tshs 9.1068 per litre to Tshs 14.068, Yona said.
Exise duty on liquefied petroleum gas (LPG) would also rise to Tshs 12 per kg from Tshs 7.1875.
A five percent sales tax on gas oil would be introduced in addition to increases in the national road toll.

"Increases in fuel prices upset everything -- transport costs, machinery costs, even fertiliser which has to be moved from the ports," Tanzanian Chamber of Commerce, Industries and Agriculture (TCCIA) Executive Director, Mariot Kalanje, told Reuters.

"A fuel cost increase will have a negative impact on the rural population...The main problem among the rural population is they depend so much on trucking for transport. Most rural communities are far away from their main sources of inputs which have to be transported," Kalanje said.
Elsewhere in the budget Yona said vehicle import taxes would rise but the cost of tyres and spare parts would fall.

Transport operators received some relief. Customs duty on imported heavy-duty radial tyres and spare parts would be cut from 40 to 30 percent and sales tax reduced from 30 to 20 percent and from 30 to 25 percent respectively.

Yona forecast economic growth at five percent for 1997/98 from 4.5 percent in 1996/87 and said inflation, which averaged 27.4 percent in 1995 and 21 percent in 1996, would continue its downward trend.
Excluding the effects of drought, year-on-year inflation was running at 13.2 percent and could reach 10 percent by June, 1998, he said.
